title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics so the same single generator output per task was used for both conditions. Execution completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 400) and consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the primary validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this curated task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, concrete execution accounting, representative diagnostics, the preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) with analysis/contamination_summary.csv reporting zero disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative LLMs promises productivity gains for network operations but raises correctness and safety concerns: incorrect sequences, transient policy violations, or misordered operations can cause outages. Prior work therefore proposes architectures that pair LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. The marginal benefit of such an architecture depends on three operational quantities: (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures produced by the chosen model and prompting policy; (ii) validator coverage and fidelity to device/emulator behavior; and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We asked a focused, preregistered confirmatory question: does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?
sections.related_work: Empirical and survey literature documents two recurring facts relevant to our study. First, LLMs produce factual errors and exhibit prompt sensitivity and sampling non‑determinism; mitigation proposals include grounding (RAG), verifier‑assisted repair, and constrained/guarded agent architectures. Second, NetOps prototypes show feasibility of intent→configuration synthesis but often lack production‑like, instrumented failure‑rate studies. Architectures that combine LLM generation with deterministic network validators (for example, Batfish‑style checkers) and automated repair loops have been proposed to improve safety; red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies further show that tool descriptions, persona/history, or tool‑chaining can substantially alter safety outcomes. These prior findings motivate preregistered, externally‑auditable measurement that isolates the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair under a fixed generator and prompt policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The experiment was preregistered (study id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) as a paired confirmatory design with n = 200 tasks, a single primary test (exact McNemar two‑sided, α = 0.05), and explicit stopping/model‑call caps (maximum_model_calls = 400: one initial generation per task plus up to one repair call if validation failed). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; 95% CIs were computed via bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). All design choices (inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness plan, contamination checks, and single repair attempt budget) were frozen before any model call and archived in the preregistration manifest.

Task bank, validators, and holdout. The confirmatory sample comprised a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Tasks encode initial/expected final state, per‑task workflow constraints (make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields, atomic paired changes), and an explicit required_sequence that the primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces. A Mininet data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the executed contamination artifact (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) records zero disagreements on that holdout.

Adapter enforcement and shared_initial semantics. To isolate the marginal effect of adding validation+repair, the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single deterministic initial LLM output was produced (adapter accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}) and reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This design removes per‑condition sampling variance and focuses the comparison on whether a validator+repair applied to the same candidate changes the pass/fail outcome. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM if the validator reported violations; up to 200 repair calls were therefore permitted but only if initial candidates failed validation.

Execution accounting and artifact handling. The run executed autonomously under the frozen plan. All model calls, prompts, validator traces, emulator traces (holdout), provider accounting, and analysis artifacts were recorded and archived. Primary analysis was executed by paired_binary_analysis_v1 on the raw paired episodes. Reproducibility artifacts include analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/missingness_summary.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv, and deterministically reconciled provider accounting.
sections.results:
Execution outcomes and primary inferential result. The run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 and complete_pair_count = 200. The adapter recorded model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued (repair_calls_used = 0) because every initial candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0); guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Statistical analysis. With zero discordant pairs the paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is logically untestable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity, contamination checks, and representative diagnostics. Because every initial candidate passed the primary validator, the GVR pipeline never invoked the repair budget and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed and analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero validator–emulator disagreements, indicating no observed validator blind spots on the tested holdout. Representative validator traces (e.g., several archived task records) show parsed_command_count and required_command_count consistent with medium‑to‑very_hard workflow constraints (make_before_break, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) while still producing validator‑satisfying sequences (validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, violation_count = 0). Provider accounting artifacts confirm the shared_initial design (cache_miss_count = 200; cache_hit_count = 0; hosted_model_call_event_count = 200).

Uninvoked sensitivity branches and empty secondary estimands. The preregistration specified sensitivity analyses for contamination flags and alternative missingness treatments; none were invoked because no tasks were flagged and no episodes failed. Secondary/exploratory estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) are not computed because no repair attempts occurred; secondary_results are empty in the analysis bundle.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation and operational lesson. The degenerate null outcome is an operationally informative result: when the selected model, prompt policy, and adapter produce validator‑passing candidates across a workload, an additional validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This does not imply GVR is unnecessary in general; rather, it emphasizes that GVR’s marginal utility is workload‑dependent. Before deploying automated repair, practitioners should measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workloads and assess validator fidelity with end‑to‑end emulation.

Why baseline failures were zero on this bank. Artifact‑grounded explanations include: (1) the prompt template and the shared_initial deterministic sampling policy encouraged succinct, constraint‑compliant sequences that matched task required_sequences; (2) the curated task bank encodes explicit workflow constraints (required_sequence) that directly map to validator checks and are therefore easier for a constrained prompt policy to satisfy; (3) the primary validator enforces the task‑encoded syntactic and intent constraints but may omit deeper device idiosyncrasies detectable only by richer emulation or real hardware; and (4) the single repair budget and shared_initial design removed per‑condition re‑sampling as a route to produce alternative repairable outputs.

Implications for evaluation design. Confirmatory studies of GVR effectiveness must ensure the chosen workload exhibits nontrivial baseline validator failure prevalence (or allow multiple generator draws per condition) if the goal is to measure a positive marginal effect. When baseline failures are rare, resources may be better spent on improving validator fidelity (device semantics, vendor idiosyncrasies), increasing generation diversity (multi‑sample or multi‑model), adversarial testing, or integrating human approval.

Reproducibility gap and mitigation. All major artifacts are archived and referenced. One remaining reproducibility gap is the absence of an explicitly labeled randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check; although analysis/contamination_summary.csv shows the holdout size and reports zero disagreements (holdout = 20 tasks), the missing labeled seed prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact drawn holdout. We disclose this gap and retain the contamination summary evidence that no disagreements were observed.

Threats to validity (brief). Internal validity: preregistration and deterministic adapter enforcement reduce post‑hoc bias but the shared_initial design trades generality for control by eliminating per‑condition sampling variance. Construct validity: the primary validator checks task‑encoded constraints but may not capture some end‑to‑end device behaviors. External validity: single model (gpt‑5‑mini), single sampling policy (shared initial), curated task bank, and single repair budget limit generalizability. Conclusion validity: the primary McNemar test is uninformative when discordant pairs are zero; nevertheless reporting the observed degenerate contingency is useful to guide future workload selection and power planning.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under adapter‑enforced shared_initial semantics. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was therefore not testable on this task bank because the baseline failure rate was 0%. This artifact‑grounded null outcome highlights that the marginal operational value of automated repair depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator fidelity. Future experimental work should (a) evaluate workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, (b) extend validator fidelity with richer emulation or real devices, (c) test multi‑sample/multi‑model generation policies, and (d) explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets. All execution and analysis artifacts referenced in this manuscript are archived for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02 and used the hosted model declared as gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) and its result is recorded in analysis/contamination_summary.csv (no disagreements observed). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared_initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite analysis/contamination_summary.csv reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (provider accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
